transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I guess I’m here because I keep forgetting things I really shouldn’t be forgetting. Like heart follow-up appointments, or I’m supposed to call the clinic back and then the whole day goes by. And I’ll show up to help with some repair—well, I’m not working now, but I still do little fixes here and there—and I’ll get there without the right tools. Then I’m standing there thinking, “How did I manage to leave that behind?” It’s been happening enough that it’s worrying me.
When did you first start noticing these memory lapses, and has it been a gradual change over months or years, or did it come on more suddenly?

It wasn’t all at once, no. I’d say it’s been really causing trouble for maybe a year and a couple months now. It kind of started after that heart scare I had, when I had to cut back on my walking and little projects and things like that. Those used to keep me… I don’t know, more settled, I guess. Since then it’s been more noticeable.
Over the past year, have you noticed a change in your mood, like feeling sad, down, or losing interest in things you used to enjoy?

I don’t know that I’d call it sad, exactly. I mean, everybody has off days, right? Some mornings I wake up and think, “Well, what was I supposed to do today?” and then I get sidetracked making coffee or looking for something in the garage. I used to enjoy keeping busy, doing little things around the house, talking to people at the hardware store—though that place changed owners and they moved everything around, which drives me nuts.

But mood-wise… I’m not sure. I haven’t really thought of it as being down or anything. I guess I’d have to think about what you mean by losing interest.
Have these memory lapses caused any real problems in managing things like your medications, finances, or other daily responsibilities on your own?

Yeah, I mean… not so much finances, I don’t think, but daily responsibilities, yes. The repair group at the senior center, they used to be able to count on me for little jobs, and now I’ll forget something or not show up when I said I would, or I’ll have the wrong stuff with me. That’s embarrassing, because I’ve always been pretty handy.

And my doctor’s office has had to call after me about the heart follow-ups I missed. They’re nice about it, but you can tell it’s a problem when they’re chasing you instead of the other way around.

Do these memory and confusion problems tend to come and go—like being much worse at certain times of day or on certain days—or have they been fairly constant and steadily present regardless of time of day?

I’m not sure I’ve noticed a real pattern like that. Some days are better than others, I guess, but I couldn’t tell you if it’s mornings or evenings. Mornings can get away from me because I start one thing and then notice something else—like I’ll go to check the calendar and end up straightening a drawer, which is ridiculous because that drawer’s been messy for ten years.

But as far as it being, you know, suddenly worse at a certain time of day… I don’t know. I haven’t really kept track of it that way.
Over this past year, would you say your memory and forgetfulness have been gradually getting worse, or have they stayed roughly the same since they started?

I’d say it’s been trouble for… a little over a year now, maybe a year and two months. It really started being noticeable after that heart scare I had, when I had to cut back on my walking and the little projects I used to do. Those things kind of kept me settled, you know?

Since then it feels like the forgetfulness has caused more real problems. I don’t know if it’s every single week getting worse in a straight line, but compared to before that, yeah, it’s definitely not the same.
Besides forgetting things, have you noticed any new difficulty finding the right words when speaking, or getting confused about directions or getting lost in places you know well?

I don’t know that I’ve noticed that, exactly. I mean, everybody loses a word now and then — I’ll be talking and the name of a tool or someone from the center just won’t pop up right away, but then usually it does later, like when I’m making coffee or something.

As far as getting lost… not really, I don’t think. I still know where I’m going in places I know. Though I do sometimes take the long way because I get thinking about something else, and then I’m like, “Why did I come down this street?” But that’s not the same as being lost, I guess.
Since your heart problem started, have you had any episodes of sudden weakness, numbness, vision changes, or trouble speaking on one side of your body, even briefly?

Not that I can think of, no. I mean, I’ve had moments where I feel off and then I start worrying because after the heart thing you notice every little twinge, you know? Like I’ll be sitting there and think, “Was that something?” and then I’m up checking the mail or I remember I left the kettle on—well, not on, just sitting there.

But one side going weak or numb, or suddenly not being able to talk right… I don’t think I’ve had anything like that. Vision changes, I’m not sure what you mean exactly, but nothing sudden like that that I remember.
Do you currently manage your own medications and bills entirely by yourself, or has anyone had to step in to help you keep track of those tasks?

Well, that’s kind of what brought me in, honestly. I try to keep track of things, but I keep forgetting stuff I really shouldn’t — like heart follow-up appointments, or that I was supposed to call the clinic back.

And then with little repair things, I’ll show up and realize I didn’t bring the right tools, which is embarrassing because I’ve done that kind of thing for years. I’ll have the wrench but not the bit I actually needed, or I’ll remember it when I’m already halfway across town. It’s not just “where did I put my glasses,” you know? It’s things that actually matter.

Has anyone actually had to take over completing any of your daily tasks—like paying a bill for you or managing your medications—or do you still get everything done yourself, even if it takes extra effort or reminders?

No, nobody’s fully taken over like that… not like they’re sitting down and doing it all for me. I’m still trying to handle things myself.

It’s more that I keep dropping the ball on things I shouldn’t — like the heart follow-up, or I’m supposed to call the clinic back and then the whole day goes by. Or I’ll go to do a repair job and get there without the right tools, which really bothers me because I used to be pretty good about that. I’ll have half of what I need, then realize the important bit is still sitting at home. So I get it done eventually, but it takes more effort and I need reminders more than I used to.

Have you noticed any new difficulty with tasks that require several steps or planning ahead, like following a recipe with multiple steps, planning a route for errands, or organizing a project you used to do easily?

Yeah… I think so, but it’s hard to say it cleanly. It’s not like I can’t do things, it’s more I lose pieces of the plan. Like what brought me in is I keep forgetting things I really shouldn’t — heart follow-up appointments, calling the clinic back, that kind of thing.

And with repair stuff, I’ll think I’ve got it all sorted, then I show up and I’ve brought the wrong tools or forgot the one thing I actually needed. I used to be better about that. Then I get irritated and start thinking about how I should’ve made a list, but of course the list is on the kitchen counter or I never made it in the first place. So, planning ahead, yeah, that’s been harder.

Looking back over the past year, has your memory and thinking gotten worse in sudden, noticeable jumps—where you seem to drop to a new, lower level all at once—or has it felt more like a smooth, gradual slide downward the whole time?

I’m not sure I can say it was sudden like a cliff, no. I mean… I don’t remember waking up one week and thinking, “Oh, I’m worse now.”

It’s more that I notice things after the fact, if that makes sense. Like I’ll realize I’ve messed something up and then start thinking, “Has this been happening more?” But I couldn’t point to a jump or a specific time it changed. Time gets slippery too—last spring versus last fall, I mix that up when I’m trying to explain it.

So… I guess I haven’t noticed any big sudden drops. It just feels like problems showing up here and there, and then I look back and wonder how long it’s been going on.
During your heart scare, did you experience any loss of consciousness, cardiac arrest, or a period where your oxygen levels or blood pressure dropped significantly?

I’m not really sure, honestly. Nobody explained it to me in a way that stuck, if they did. I don’t remember anyone saying “cardiac arrest” or anything like that, but I also get mixed up when there’s a lot going on and people are coming in and out.

I mean, during that whole heart scare I was more focused on just getting through it, and then later I’d think, “Wait, what exactly did they say happened?” So… I don’t know about oxygen levels or blood pressure dropping. I’d probably have to look at the paperwork, if I can find where I put it.
Since that initial heart scare, have your memory and thinking problems leveled off and stayed about the same, or have they kept getting worse even without any new heart issues?

I’d say it’s been real trouble for… about a year and a couple months, I think. Since that heart scare, really, because after that I had to cut back on walking and the little projects I used to do, and those things kind of kept me steady, you know?

As far as whether it leveled off or kept getting worse… I don’t know if I can measure it that neatly. It feels like since then it’s been more noticeable and more in the way. Not like I can point to a brand-new heart thing causing it, just that after I stopped doing my usual walking and projects, the memory and planning stuff started causing actual problems.
Do you have a history of high blood pressure, diabetes, or any prior strokes or mini-strokes that a doctor has told you about?

I don’t think anyone’s told me I had a stroke or one of those mini-strokes, at least not that I remember. With the blood pressure and diabetes… I get mixed up with what all the numbers mean. They take your blood pressure every time and say things fast, and then I’m thinking about where I parked or whether I brought the right papers.

So I can’t give you a clean yes-or-no on all of it. I’d probably need to look at my records or ask my regular doctor, because I don’t want to tell you wrong.
Have you noticed any new problems with your balance or the way you walk, like unsteadiness or a shuffling gait, since your heart scare?

I don’t know that I’ve noticed anything like that, not in a clear way. I mean, I’m slower than I used to be, but I’m 68, so sometimes I don’t know what’s just age and what’s something else.

Shuffling… I don’t think anyone’s told me I shuffle. I do catch myself thinking about where I’m going and then I’m already halfway across the room looking for something else, but that’s not really walking, I guess. Balance-wise, I can’t say there’s been some new thing since the heart scare that I’d point to.
Aside from these planning and memory issues, are you still able to manage basic personal care tasks—like bathing, dressing, and preparing your own meals—completely on your own without any difficulty?

I’m not sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean, those things are so routine I don’t really keep score of them, you know? Like bathing and getting dressed, I don’t sit there thinking, “Was that hard today?” unless something really goes wrong.

Meals… well, it depends what you mean by preparing, I guess. I don’t want to say it’s all completely fine if you mean every little step, but I also can’t point to some specific major problem. I’d probably need you to break down what you’re asking a little more.
